headline: Canada and the EU open talks on closer ties

chunks.text: Canada wants a closer relationship with the European Union. This week, Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke to the European [[Parliament]] in Strasbourg. He {{set out}} plans for a new economic [[partnership]] between Canada and the EU. He {{ruled out}} full membership. Canada, he said, wants "a unique [[alliance]]" instead. The two sides will {{follow up on}} the visit at a [[summit]] in Ottawa on October 29 and 30. The talks are only beginning.

verbs.wrong: To arrange a new office or system
verbs.why: The mayor set out her plans for the new park. The report sets out three ways to save money. In Strasbourg, Canada's prime minister set out plans for a new economic partnership with the EU.

verbs.correct: To say something will not happen
verbs.wrong: To make a formal decision on a case
verbs.why: The doctor ruled out surgery for now. The coach ruled out a return before June. Canada's prime minister ruled out full membership of the EU.

verbs.correct: To take the next step after something
verbs.wrong: To use something when other plans fail
verbs.why: She followed up on the job interview with an email. The police followed up on the phone tip. Canada and the EU will follow up on the Strasbourg visit at a summit in Ottawa.

chunks.text: One idea is [[labor mobility]]. Canadians could one day live and work across the EU without a [[visa]]. Carney reportedly {{brought up}} the idea with the French president. A US newspaper reported that Canada could become the first "[[associate member]]" of the EU. But no such status exists, and European [[diplomats]] {{played down}} the report. The EU [[ambassador]] to Canada said the two sides are {{working out}} something unique.

verbs.correct: To start talking about a topic
verbs.wrong: To introduce a new law or rule
verbs.why: He brought up the rent at dinner. Do not bring up politics at the party. Canada's prime minister reportedly brought up visa-free work rights with the French president.

verbs.correct: To make something seem less important
verbs.wrong: To pretend to agree with a plan
verbs.why: The company played down the size of the problem. She played down her role in the win. European diplomats played down the report about associate membership.

verbs.correct: To plan the details of something
verbs.wrong: To repay a debt through extra work
verbs.why: We are still working out the schedule for the trip. The two families worked out a plan for the summer. The EU ambassador said both sides are working out something unique.

chunks.text: Nothing is agreed yet. The EU ambassador said the Strasbourg visit would open talks, not {{wrap up}} a deal. Any deal must then go to the 27 EU [[member states]] and to Canada's [[provinces]]. Canada's [[trade deal]] with the EU has been in force since 2017. It {{cuts down on}} [[paperwork]] for [[business visitors]] and company transfers. It does not cover long-term work [[migration]]. Ten EU countries, including France and Italy, have still not {{signed off on}} it.

verbs.wrong: To protect a deal from criticism
verbs.why: Let's wrap up the meeting before lunch. They wrapped up the project a week early. The EU ambassador said the visit would open talks, not wrap up a deal.

verbs.correct: To reduce the amount of something
verbs.wrong: To stop a supply of something
verbs.why: I am trying to cut down on coffee. The office cut down on printing last year. The 2017 trade deal cuts down on paperwork for business visitors.

verbs.correct: To give official approval to something
verbs.wrong: To join a program or a service
verbs.why: The manager signed off on the budget yesterday. Both parents signed off on the school trip. Ten EU countries have still not signed off on the trade deal with Canada.

chunks.text: For ordinary workers, the short-term gains are modest. Today, 22 of the 27 EU countries have [[working holiday]] agreements with Canada. A closer partnership could {{open up}} more work and study options, mainly for young people. Canada's opposition Conservatives {{pushed back}}, and one Conservative [[lawmaker]] warned about immigration. In a March [[survey]], 25 percent of Canadians supported formal EU membership, and 58 percent called it worth exploring. Anyone planning a move should {{hold off}}. Talks like these often {{drag on}} for years.

verbs.correct: To create new chances for people
verbs.wrong: To admit that you made a mistake
verbs.why: The new bridge opened up jobs on both sides of the river. Online classes open up study options for parents. A closer partnership could open up more work and study options for young Canadians.

verbs.correct: To resist or oppose a plan
verbs.wrong: To take the lead in a project
verbs.why: Parents pushed back against the longer school day. The staff pushed back when the office moved. Canada's opposition Conservatives pushed back against the EU plan.

verbs.wrong: To keep something you already have
verbs.why: We held off on buying a car until prices fell. Hold off on the email until the boss agrees. Anyone planning a move to Europe should hold off for now.

verbs.wrong: To pull someone into a dispute
verbs.why: The meeting dragged on for three hours. The road repairs dragged on all summer. Talks between Canada and the EU could drag on for years.

mainIdea.s: Canada's prime minister has opened talks on a closer partnership with the EU that could include work rights. Nothing is agreed, and any deal must pass 27 countries and the provinces.
mainIdea.why: The Strasbourg visit opened talks, mobility is only one idea under discussion, and member states and provinces still need to approve any deal.

mainIdea.s: Canada and the EU have agreed that Canadians can live and work in Europe without a visa. The deal now only needs approval from all ten provinces before it starts early next year.
mainIdea.why: Close, but nothing has been agreed. Visa-free work rights are only an idea being discussed, and the talks are at the very start.

mainIdea.s: Canada has finally persuaded the last ten EU countries to approve the 2017 trade deal. Business visitors will now face faster entry and far fewer forms on both sides of the ocean.
mainIdea.why: Ten EU countries, including France and Italy, still have not signed off on the trade deal. The news is about new talks, not that old approval.

tf.s: Canada's prime minister ruled out full membership of the EU.
tf.why: He said Canada wants a unique alliance instead of membership.

tf.s: The two sides will follow up on the visit at a summit in Brussels.
tf.why: The summit is in Ottawa, on October 29 and 30.

tf.s: European diplomats played down the report about associate membership.
tf.why: No such status exists today, so diplomats treated the newspaper report as a distraction.

tf.s: Ten EU countries have still not signed off on the 2017 trade deal.
tf.why: France and Italy are among the countries that have not given approval.

tf.s: The 2017 trade deal cuts down on paperwork for long-term work migration.
tf.why: It cuts down on paperwork for business visitors and company transfers. Long-term work migration is not covered.

tf.s: A March survey found that 58 percent of Canadians support formal EU membership.
tf.why: Only 25 percent support formal membership. The 58 percent only called the idea worth exploring, and the opposition Conservatives pushed back against it.
